title: Cross-Tenant / Multi-Tenant Access-Control Testing
summary: The SaaS-specific slice of broken object-level authorization: whether one tenant/organization can reach another tenant's data or actions. Distinct from generic IDOR in that the boundary under test is the TENANT, and the highest-value tests use a two-account (tenant A vs tenant B) setup plus header/claim scoping abuse. Lead with this on any multi-tenant SaaS target.

steps.text: Provision two isolated tenants: attacker in org B, victim in org A. Every finding must be an org-B session touching an org-A object — that separation is the proof.
While logged into org A, catalogue object ids (org id, project/record/file/invoice ids, user ids). These become the org-A targets you replay from org B.
Replay an org-A object id with org-B credentials. A 200 with org-A data is confirmed cross-tenant read.
Test cross-tenant WRITE/DELETE, not just read — isolation is often enforced on GET but forgotten on PATCH/DELETE, and cross-tenant mutation is Critical.
Abuse trusted tenant-scoping inputs: override the tenant via a header, body field, or JWT claim the server trusts instead of deriving from the session.
Sweep the whole app with Burp Autorize: set org-B's session as the low-priv identity, browse as org A; Autorize replays each request as org B and flags 'Authorization bypassed!'.
Enumerate sequential/guessable org or object ids to harvest other tenants at scale; diff status/length.

Harvest ids that leak across the tenant boundary — list endpoints, search, notification emails, exports, referers — then replay them cross-tenant. Don't assume UUIDs are safe; they leak and UUIDv1 is predictable.
GraphQL: global node(id:) lookups and batched queries frequently bypass per-tenant checks REST enforces.

code.cmd:
curl -s https://target/graphql -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TENANT_B_TOKEN>' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query":"{ node(id:\"<ORG_A_GID>\"){ ... on Invoice { id total } } }"}'

steps.text: Report: name both tenants, the object, read vs write, and whether cross-tenant. Cross-tenant write/delete = Critical; cross-tenant read of sensitive data = High. See also the generic Insecure Direct Object References entry.

title: Webhook Security Testing (SSRF, Secret Leakage, Signature Bypass, Replay)
summary: User-configurable webhooks are a rich, under-tested SaaS surface. The server makes an outbound request to a URL the user controls, making webhooks a first-class SSRF primitive; the shared signing secret and its verification are also frequently mishandled. Test the outbound side (SSRF/metadata), the secret side (leakage, weak/optional signatures), and delivery (replay).

steps.text: Find every webhook config: integrations, CI/CD notifications, outgoing-webhook/callback URL fields, OAuth-app registration URLs, per-repo/per-project hooks.
SSRF via the webhook URL — point it at an OOB canary to confirm server-side fetch, then at internal/metadata targets.

code.cmd:
# webhook target -> your collaborator/interactsh host, then trigger an event
http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/  (Metadata-Flavor: Google)

steps.text: Defeat naive host filters with alternate encodings / rebinding.

code.cmd:
http://127.1  http://0x7f000001  http://[::1]  http://2130706433
# or a rebinding host resolving to 169.254.169.254

steps.text: Stand up a listener as the webhook target and read exactly what the server sends — signature header name, and any secret/token leaked in headers or body.

code.cmd: python3 -m http.server 8000   # or: ngrok http 8000 and read the inspector

steps.text: Test signature verification: (a) remove the signature header, (b) send garbage, (c) flip the payload but keep the old signature. Any accepted variant = broken verification / forgeable deliveries.

code.cmd:
curl -s -X POST https://target/webhooks/incoming/<id> \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"event":"payment.succeeded","amount":0}'   # NO signature header

steps.text: Hunt the signing secret: UI pre-filled fields, API responses that echo config, exported settings, verbose errors. A leaked secret lets you forge valid signatures.
Replay a captured signed delivery — no timestamp/nonce check means replaying 'payment.succeeded'/'subscription.active' can grant entitlements or duplicate side effects.
If the app parses/reflects the webhook RESPONSE body, a malicious receiver can inject back into the app (stored XSS, XXE on an XML response, deserialization).
Report with OOB proof (collaborator hit + source IP proving server-side origin), the internal resource reached, and whether signatures/replay protection are enforced.

title: Broken Function-Level Authorization (BFLA / Privileged-Function Access)
summary: OWASP API5:2023. Where BOLA is about objects, BFLA is about ACTIONS: a low-privileged or regular user invoking administrative or higher-role FUNCTIONS (create-user, change-role, delete-tenant, export-all, feature-flags). The gap is an endpoint that checks authentication but not the caller's ROLE. Test by taking privileged calls captured as an admin and replaying them as a normal user, and by guessing admin routes/verbs.

steps.text: Enumerate privileged functions. If you can access an admin/staff account (or docs/JS), catalogue every administrative action and its exact request (method, path, body). These are your BFLA candidates to replay as a low-priv user.
Replay an admin action with a NORMAL user's session. A 200/side-effect is confirmed BFLA.
Swap the HTTP verb. Authz is often enforced per (path, method); a route that blocks GET may allow PUT/DELETE/PATCH. Also try method-override headers.

code.cmd:
curl -s -X DELETE https://target/api/projects/123 -H 'Authorization: Bearer <NORMAL_TOKEN>' -i
curl -s -X POST   https://target/api/projects/123 -H 'X-HTTP-Method-Override: DELETE' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <NORMAL_TOKEN>' -i

steps.text: Guess admin routes even without an admin account. Diff /api/user/* vs /api/admin/*, try common privileged verbs and console paths.

Attack role/scope inputs the server trusts: a role in the body, a claim in the JWT, or a header (X-Role, X-Admin). Downgrade/upgrade and see if the server honors it instead of deriving role server-side.
Mass-assign a privilege field during normal create/update (register or profile-edit) to grant yourself a role — the write-side twin of BFLA.

Automate with Burp Autorize: set the NORMAL user as the low-priv identity, then browse the app as admin. Autorize replays every admin request as the normal user and flags 'Authorization bypassed!' across the whole console at once.
Check GraphQL mutations — admin mutations (deleteOrg, setRole) frequently lack the per-field authz that REST admin routes have.

code.cmd:
curl -s https://target/graphql -H 'Authorization: Bearer <NORMAL_TOKEN>' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query":"mutation{ setUserRole(id:1, role:ADMIN){ id role } }"}'

steps.text: Report: name the privileged function, the low-priv identity used, and the effect (account creation, role change, data export, tenant delete). Admin-function access as a normal user is typically High–Critical. Pairs with the cross-tenant/BOLA entry for full authz coverage.

title: HTTP Host Header Attacks (Reset Poisoning, Routing SSRF, Cache Poisoning)
summary: Many apps trust the Host header (or X-Forwarded-Host) to build absolute URLs, route requests, or key caches. Tampering with it enables password-reset poisoning (reset link points to attacker), web cache poisoning, routing-based SSRF to internal vhosts, and occasional authentication/ACL bypasses. Always test both the real Host header and the X-Forwarded-* family.

steps.text: Baseline: can you change Host and still get a 200? If the app serves normally with an arbitrary Host, it isn't validating it — every test below is in play.
Password-reset poisoning: trigger a reset and override the Host so the emailed link points to your server — capturing the victim's token when they click.
If Host is validated, try the override headers apps commonly trust instead.
Routing-based SSRF: some front-ends route by Host to an internal vhost. Point Host at internal names / metadata and watch for internal responses or timing.
Web cache poisoning via Host / X-Forwarded-Host: if the cache keys on path but the response reflects the header into an absolute URL/script src, poison it for all users.

code.cmd: curl -s https://target/resource.js -H 'X-Forwarded-Host: evil.com' -i   # look for evil.com reflected + a cache HIT

steps.text: Try duplicate/ambiguous Host headers and absolute-URI request lines to bypass naive validation (front-end and back-end may disagree on which Host wins).

code.cmd:
printf 'GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: target
Host: evil.com

'   # send via Burp/nc; observe which Host is used

steps.text: Authentication/ACL bypass: internal-only or admin panels sometimes gate on Host (e.g. Host: internal). Spoof it to reach restricted areas.
Enumerate virtual hosts on the same IP to find hidden apps (staging, admin) that only answer to a specific Host.
Report the concrete impact: a captured reset token, a poisoned cached response served to another client, or an internal resource reached. Reset poisoning and cache poisoning are typically High.

title: Obfuscation — how it works and how it is detected
summary: Encoding, packing and command-line mangling change what a payload LOOKS like without changing what it DOES. Detection therefore moves from the string to the shape: the encoding itself is the signal, and the payload has to decode before it can run.

steps.text: Confirm process-creation events carry the FULL command line (Windows 4688 with 'Include command line' enabled, Sysmon EID 1, auditd execve).
Confirm PowerShell script-block logging (4104) is on and forwarded — it records the deobfuscated script and is the strongest single control for this family.
Baseline command-line length and entropy per host role; alert on outliers rather than on specific decoded strings.
Check that AMSI events and Defender detections are collected, not just acted on locally.
For the packing variant, alert on high-entropy executables written to user-writable paths and then executed (Sysmon 11 followed by 1).

> **How to read this page.** This is a DEFENDER'S reference. It explains what this family of technique is and why it works — enough to recognise it — and then spends most of its length on how it is *detected* and what removes it. It is deliberately not a recipe: there are no commands here, and it will not tell you how to evade anything. If you are testing, the value is knowing what you would be leaving behind; if you are defending, the value is the telemetry and the controls.

## What it is

Obfuscation is any transformation that preserves behaviour while destroying the literal text a
signature was written against: base64 or hex encoding, string concatenation and reordering,
character substitution, environment-variable indirection, packing/crypting a binary, and
command-line mangling. ATT&CK groups these under [T1027 Obfuscated Files or
Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027) with sub-techniques for [Software Packing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/002) and
[Command Obfuscation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/010), all under the **Stealth** tactic (TA0005 — the tactic
older matrices called Defense Evasion).

## Why it works

Static signatures match bytes. If the bytes change, the signature misses. That is the entire
mechanism, and it is also the entire weakness.

## Why it usually fails

Obfuscated content has to be *deobfuscated to execute* — ATT&CK tracks that step separately as
[T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1140). So there are two independent
detection surfaces:

1. **The obfuscation is itself anomalous.** Normal administrative commands are not 400
   characters of base64. High-entropy command lines, unusual character-class ratios, excessive
   concatenation and reordered tokens are all measurable. Detection rules match the *encoding*,
   which means an obfuscated command line is frequently a *stronger* signal than the plain one
   would have been.
2. **The decoded form is observable at runtime.** On Windows, AMSI hands the deobfuscated script
   to the scanner immediately before execution, and PowerShell script-block logging (4104)
   records the expanded block. On Linux, `auditd` execve captures the full argv, and the shell
   history and process tree still show what actually ran.

## What a defender should collect

- **Windows Security 4688** and **Sysmon EID 1** with full command line — the encoded string is
  captured verbatim and can be decoded by the analyst or by the rule.
- **PowerShell 4103/4104** script-block logging — records the *expanded* script, defeating
  source-level obfuscation entirely. This is the single highest-value control on this page.
- **AMSI** — `AmsiScanBuffer` sees the deobfuscated buffer; Defender AMSI triggers surface as
  their own events.
- **auditd SYSCALL execve** and osquery `process_events.command_line` on Linux.
- **File entropy / packer detection** at write time for the packing variant, plus Sysmon EID 11.

## Public detections to start from

- [Suspicious Encoded PowerShell Command Line](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/windows/process_creation/proc_creation_win_powershell_base64_encoded_cmd.yml)
  — SigmaHQ `ca2092a1-c273-4878-9b4b-0d60115bf5ea`, high.
- [PowerShell ShellCode](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/windows/powershell/powershell_script/posh_ps_shellcode_b64.yml)
  — SigmaHQ `16b37b70-6fcf-4814-a092-c36bd3aafcbd`, high.
- [Powershell Token Obfuscation](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules-threat-hunting/windows/powershell/powershell_script/posh_ps_token_obfuscation.yml)
  — SigmaHQ `f3a98ce4-6164-4dd4-867c-4d83de7eca51`, medium.

## What removes the gap

Turn on script-block logging and process-creation command-line auditing everywhere. Without
them, obfuscation works because there is nothing recording the expanded form; with them, it
mostly stops mattering. Alert on encoding *shape* rather than on decoded strings.

title: In-memory execution — how it works and how it is detected
summary: Running code without writing it to disk defeats file-based scanning and forensics that start from the filesystem. It does not defeat process, memory or network telemetry — which is exactly where detection for this family lives.

steps.text: Confirm EDR memory scanning / unbacked-memory detection is enabled, not just installed.
Collect Sysmon EID 7 (image load) and alert on modules loaded by processes that have no business loading them.
Correlate the network fetch (Sysmon 3 / proxy) with the process that made it — the download step is the one part of this family that cannot stay in memory.
Hunt for RWX allocations and W->X transitions where your EDR exposes them.
Verify PowerShell 4104 and AMSI events are forwarded — in-memory loaders still pass through both.

> **How to read this page.** This is a DEFENDER'S reference. It explains what this family of technique is and why it works — enough to recognise it — and then spends most of its length on how it is *detected* and what removes it. It is deliberately not a recipe: there are no commands here, and it will not tell you how to evade anything. If you are testing, the value is knowing what you would be leaving behind; if you are defending, the value is the telemetry and the controls.

## What it is

Loading and executing code entirely in a process's memory rather than from a file on disk:
reflective loading of a module, executing a downloaded buffer, and "fileless" tradecraft
generally. ATT&CK tracks the core of it as [T1620 Reflective Code Loading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1620)
(**Stealth**, TA0005).

## Why it works

A large amount of defensive tooling is anchored to the filesystem: on-write AV scanning, hash
allowlists, file-integrity monitoring, and the forensic habit of starting from "what was
dropped". If nothing is dropped, all of that has nothing to look at.

## Why it usually fails

The code still has to be *fetched*, *allocated*, and *run*, and each of those is observable:

- **Fetch** — something made a network request. Proxy, DNS and flow logs record it, and the
  requesting process is attributable (Sysmon EID 3 / auditd connect).
- **Allocate** — memory has to be made writable and then executable. RWX allocations, and the
  W→X transition, are anomalous in most normal software and are precisely what EDR memory
  telemetry watches.
- **Run** — a module appears in a process that has no file backing it. "Unbacked" or "floating"
  executable memory is one of the highest-fidelity signals available, because legitimate code
  almost always has an image on disk behind it.

Fileless is a statement about disk. It is not a statement about memory, process or network.

## What a defender should collect

- **EDR memory scanning / unbacked-executable-memory detection** — the primary control here.
  If you have EDR, this is the setting to confirm is enabled.
- **Sysmon EID 7** (image load) — spot modules loaded into processes that never load them,
  and modules with no corresponding file.
- **Sysmon EID 8/10** (remote thread, process access) for the injection variants.
- **Sysmon EID 3 + proxy/DNS logs** — the fetch is the one step that leaves the process entirely.
- **PowerShell 4104** — in-memory .NET and script loaders still show up in script-block logs.
- **AMSI** — buffers scanned before execution regardless of where they came from.

## Public detections to start from

- [Amsi.DLL Load By Uncommon Process](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules-threat-hunting/windows/image_load/image_load_dll_amsi_uncommon_process.yml)
  — SigmaHQ `facd1549-e416-48e0-b8c4-41d7215eedc8`, low (hunting).
- [CreateRemoteThread API and LoadLibrary](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules-threat-hunting/windows/create_remote_thread/create_remote_thread_win_loadlibrary.yml)
  — SigmaHQ `052ec6f6-1adc-41e6-907a-f1c813478bee`, medium.

## What removes the gap

Enable EDR memory telemetry and image-load logging; treat "executable memory with no file behind
it" as a first-class alert. Constrained-language mode and application control (WDAC/AppLocker)
raise the cost sharply because the loader itself becomes the thing that is blocked.

title: Process injection — how it works and how it is detected
summary: Running code inside another process borrows that process's identity and trust. The cross-process operations required to do it are rare, well-instrumented, and among the highest-fidelity detections available on Windows.

steps.text: Confirm Sysmon EID 10 (ProcessAccess) is collected WITH the granted-access mask, and EID 8 (CreateRemoteThread) is not filtered out wholesale for volume.
Baseline the legitimate injector source->target pairs in your estate so the rare genuine cases don't force you to disable the rule.
Alert on handles opened to LSASS with VM_READ/QUERY rights from unexpected images.
Hunt for processes whose in-memory image does not match the file on disk (hollowing).
Confirm PPL / credential-guard protections are on for the highest-value target processes.

> **How to read this page.** This is a DEFENDER'S reference. It explains what this family of technique is and why it works — enough to recognise it — and then spends most of its length on how it is *detected* and what removes it. It is deliberately not a recipe: there are no commands here, and it will not tell you how to evade anything. If you are testing, the value is knowing what you would be leaving behind; if you are defending, the value is the telemetry and the controls.

## What it is

Executing code in the address space of a process you did not start, so the code inherits that
process's identity, network reputation and parent-child plausibility. ATT&CK: [T1055 Process
Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055) (**Stealth** + Privilege Escalation), with sub-techniques including
[DLL Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/001) and [Process Hollowing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/012). Closely related is
[T1134 Access Token Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134).

## Why it works

Detection and policy are frequently anchored to the *process*: which binary, which parent, which
user, which network reputation. Injection decouples the code from the process it runs in, so all
of those answers become wrong.

## Why it usually fails

Injection requires a specific, unusual sequence of cross-process operations, and every one of
them is instrumented:

1. **Open a handle to another process** with rights like `PROCESS_VM_WRITE`,
   `PROCESS_VM_OPERATION`, `PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD` — Sysmon EID 10 records the access and the
   granted-access mask, which is itself a strong discriminator.
2. **Write into that process's memory** and mark it executable — RWX allocations in a remote
   process are rare in benign software.
3. **Start execution** — via a remote thread (Sysmon EID 8), an APC, a hijacked thread context,
   or a hollowed-out image.

Hollowing adds its own tell: a process created suspended, its image unmapped and replaced, so the
on-disk image and the in-memory image disagree. That mismatch is directly checkable.

## What a defender should collect

- **Sysmon EID 8** (CreateRemoteThread) and **EID 10** (ProcessAccess) with granted-access masks
  — the two highest-value events for this family. Tune by source/target image pairs, not by
  turning them off.
- **Sysmon EID 25** (process image tampering) for hollowing/herpaderping-style manipulation.
- **EDR behavioural detections** for cross-process memory writes and thread creation.
- **Image/memory mismatch checks** — compare the in-memory image with the file on disk.
- Note that legitimate injectors exist (some AV, accessibility and instrumentation tooling), so
  build an allow-baseline of source→target pairs rather than alerting blind.

## Public detections to start from

- [CreateRemoteThread API and LoadLibrary](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules-threat-hunting/windows/create_remote_thread/create_remote_thread_win_loadlibrary.yml)
  — SigmaHQ `052ec6f6-1adc-41e6-907a-f1c813478bee`, medium.
- [HackTool - Potential CobaltStrike Process Injection](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/windows/create_remote_thread/create_remote_thread_win_hktl_cobaltstrike.yml)
  — SigmaHQ `6309645e-122d-4c5b-bb2b-22e4f9c2fa42`, high.
- [HackTool - HollowReaper Execution](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/windows/process_creation/proc_creation_win_hktl_hollowreaper.yml)
  — SigmaHQ `85d23b42-9a9d-4f8f-b3d7-d2733c1d58f5`, high.

## What removes the gap

Turn on Sysmon EID 8 and 10 (many default configs trim them for volume — trim by *filter*, not by
removing the event) and baseline the legitimate source→target pairs in your estate. Protected
Process Light for LSASS and credential-guard-style protections remove the highest-value targets
from reach entirely.

title: AMSI / ETW tampering — how it works and how it is detected
summary: Interfering with the sensors themselves — the scan interface and the event pipeline — is tracked by ATT&CK as Defense Impairment. It is loud in a specific way: the SILENCE is the signal, and turning a sensor off is itself an event.

steps.text: Alert on Security 1102 and 1100 unconditionally — no tuning, no exceptions.
Forward logs off-host in near-real-time so local tampering cannot retract them.
Monitor per-host telemetry VOLUME and agent heartbeat; a host going quiet is the signal.
Enable vendor tamper protection so stopping/altering the security service fails and is logged.
Hunt for amsi.dll loaded by unusual processes and for registry writes under security-product keys (Sysmon 13/14).

> **How to read this page.** This is a DEFENDER'S reference. It explains what this family of technique is and why it works — enough to recognise it — and then spends most of its length on how it is *detected* and what removes it. It is deliberately not a recipe: there are no commands here, and it will not tell you how to evade anything. If you are testing, the value is knowing what you would be leaving behind; if you are defending, the value is the telemetry and the controls.

## What it is

Degrading the host's own instrumentation so that later actions are not recorded: patching or
disabling the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI), unhooking or silencing Event Tracing for
Windows (ETW) providers, stopping or blinding security services, and clearing logs. ATT&CK
places these under **Defense Impairment** (TA0112) — [T1685 Disable or Modify
Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1685), [T1112 Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [T1690 Prevent Command History
Logging](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1690) — and [T1070 Indicator Removal](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1070) under Stealth.

## Why it works

Almost every other detection on this page depends on a sensor being alive. If the sensor is
disabled before the noisy action happens, the noisy action produces nothing.

## Why it usually fails

Three independent reasons, and they compound:

1. **Turning a sensor off is itself an event.** Clearing the Windows event log writes **Security
   1102** *before* the log is emptied. Stopping a service writes **System 7036/7045**. Registry
   changes to security-product keys write **Sysmon 13/14**. The tamper is recorded by the thing
   being tampered with, on its way out.
2. **The logs have usually already left.** Anything forwarded to a SIEM, a WEF collector or an
   EDR cloud is beyond reach the moment it is shipped. Local tampering does not retract it.
3. **Silence is measurable.** A host that reliably emits telemetry and then stops is an alert in
   its own right. Absence-of-heartbeat detection turns the whole technique into a signal.

## What a defender should collect

- **Security 1102** (audit log cleared) and **1100** (event log service shut down) — treat both
  as high severity, always.
- **System 7045 / 7036** — service installation and state changes for security products.
- **Sysmon 13/14** — registry writes under security-product and AMSI-related keys.
- **Sysmon 7** — `amsi.dll` loaded by a process that has no reason to load it, a classic
  hunting signal.
- **EDR/agent heartbeat and log-volume monitoring** — alert on a host going quiet, per host and
  per source.
- **`auditd` CONFIG_CHANGE** and execve of `systemctl stop` / `kill` against security daemons on
  Linux; `HISTFILE`/`HISTCONTROL` manipulation for the shell-history variant.

## Public detections to start from

- [Amsi.DLL Load By Uncommon Process](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules-threat-hunting/windows/image_load/image_load_dll_amsi_uncommon_process.yml)
  — SigmaHQ `facd1549-e416-48e0-b8c4-41d7215eedc8`, low (hunting).
- [Windows Defender AMSI Trigger Detected](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/windows/builtin/windefend/win_defender_malware_detected_amsi_source.yml)
  — SigmaHQ `ea9bf0fa-edec-4fb8-8b78-b119f2528186`, high.

## A note for testers

Impairing a customer's security instrumentation is destructive to *evidence*, not just to
detection, and it is out of keeping with an authorized test unless the scope explicitly asks for
a detection-response exercise. HackPit's cockpit flags commands of this shape so the choice is
never accidental.

## What removes the gap

Forward logs off the host immediately (WEF/SIEM/EDR cloud), alert on 1102/1100 unconditionally,
monitor agent heartbeats, and protect security-service configuration with tamper protection so
the attempt fails *and* is recorded.

title: Living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins) — how it works and how it is detected
summary: Using signed, built-in system binaries to do the work means nothing unusual is installed and nothing fails an allowlist. Detection shifts entirely from WHAT ran to HOW it ran — the parent, the arguments, and what it did next.

steps.text: Confirm process-creation logging captures the PARENT image as well as the command line — without it this family is largely invisible.
Baseline parent->child pairs per host role; alert on office suite, web server and database processes spawning interpreters or LOLBins.
Alert on signed system binaries making outbound network connections (Sysmon 1 + 3).
Track per-host frequency for each LOLBin — most are near-zero on a given role, so rarity alone is a usable detection.
Deploy WDAC/AppLocker rules that block the misuse path (remote scriptlets, remote content) rather than trying to block the binary itself.

## What it is

Achieving execution, download or persistence through binaries that ship with the operating
system and are already trusted — the Windows LOLBAS set (`rundll32`, `regsvr32`, `mshta`,
`certutil`, `msbuild`, `wmic`, …) and the Unix GTFOBins equivalents (interpreters, editors,
archivers and setuid helpers with a shell escape). ATT&CK: [T1218 System Binary Proxy
Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218) (**Stealth**), with [Hijack Execution Flow](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574) alongside it.

## Why it works

It is aimed squarely at three specific controls:

- **Application allowlisting** — the binary is Microsoft-signed and already permitted.
- **Hash/reputation blocking** — nothing new was written, so there is nothing to look up.
- **"Unusual software installed" detections** — none was.

## Why it usually fails

Because the *identity* of the binary was never the interesting part. What matters is context,
and context is fully logged:

- **Parent-child relationships.** `winword.exe → mshta.exe`, `w3wp.exe → cmd.exe`,
  `sqlservr.exe → cmd.exe`: the child is normal, the pairing is not. This is the single most
  productive detection idea on this page.
- **Argument shape.** These binaries have narrow legitimate uses. `certutil` with `-urlcache`
  and a URL, `regsvr32` with a remote scriptlet, `rundll32` with a suspicious export — the
  arguments are the signature, and they are captured in full by process-creation logging.
- **What happened next.** A signed binary making an outbound connection to a fresh domain, or
  writing an executable into a user-writable path, is the sequence that gives it away.
- **Frequency.** Most LOLBins are near-zero-frequency on a given host role. Rarity is a
  detection.

## What a defender should collect

- **Sysmon EID 1 / Security 4688** with full command line AND parent image — without the parent,
  most of this family is invisible; with it, most of it is trivial.
- **Sysmon EID 3** — outbound connections attributed to a LOLBin process.
- **Sysmon EID 11** — files written by a LOLBin.
- **auditd execve** on Linux, plus attention to setuid helpers and interpreter invocations from
  service accounts.

## Public detections to start from

SigmaHQ carries a large body of per-binary process-creation rules under
[`rules/windows/process_creation/`](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/windows/process_creation) — the LOLBAS-shaped
ones are the direct answer to this family. A representative example:

- [Invoke-Obfuscation Via Use MSHTA - Security](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/windows/builtin/security/win_security_invoke_obfuscation_via_use_mshta_services_security.yml)
  — SigmaHQ `9b8d9203-4e0f-4cd9-bb06-4cc4ea6d0e9a`, high.

## What removes the gap

Application control that blocks the *misuse path* rather than the binary — WDAC/AppLocker rules
that stop `regsvr32`/`mshta` from executing remote content, and constrained language mode for
PowerShell. Combine with parent-child baselining per host role: the office-suite and web-server
process trees are where this shows up first.

title: Behavioural evasion (sandbox, timing, environment checks) — how it works and how it is detected
summary: Deciding not to act — because the environment looks like a sandbox, or because acting slowly stays under a threshold — targets the analysis pipeline rather than the sensor. The checks themselves are observable, and thresholds are a defender's choice, not a law.

steps.text: Add a long-window cumulative counterpart to every rate-based detection you own — pacing beats a counter, not a baseline.
Add first-seen / rarity detections (first time this account touched this host) which have no threshold to slip under.
Treat 'ran extensive environment checks, then exited' as a suspicious sandbox verdict, not a clean one.
Review telemetry RETENTION: pacing only works if the data ages out faster than the activity spreads.
Hunt for clustered environment-enumeration calls (CPU count, MAC prefix, debugger presence) in process and API telemetry.

body_md:
> **How to read this page.** This is a DEFENDER'S reference. It explains what this family of technique is and why it works — enough to recognise it — and then spends most of its length on how it is *detected* and what removes it. It is deliberately not a recipe: there are no commands here, and it will not tell you how to evade anything. If you are testing, the value is knowing what you would be leaving behind; if you are defending, the value is the telemetry and the controls.

## What it is

Two related ideas. **Sandbox / VM awareness**: probing for the signs of an analysis environment —
low core count, small disk, known MAC prefixes, analysis tooling, absent user artefacts,
accelerated clocks — and staying inert if they are found. **Timing / threshold evasion**: pacing
activity so it stays under whatever rate a detection is counting. ATT&CK:
[T1497 Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) and [T1622 Debugger Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1622),
both **Stealth** (and both also Discovery — because checking is itself reconnaissance).

## Why it works

Automated analysis has a time budget. If nothing happens within it, the sample is scored benign.
Threshold-based detections have a window and a count; activity spread thinner than the window
never trips them.

## Why it usually fails

- **The checks are the signal.** ATT&CK classes these as Discovery for a reason: enumerating CPU
  count, MAC prefixes, installed analysis tools, uptime and debugger presence is itself a
  distinctive behaviour, and it is captured in process-creation and API telemetry. A sample that
  looks hard at its environment and then does nothing is *more* interesting than one that acts.
- **Production is not a sandbox.** Inertness in the lab buys nothing on the real host, where the
  code must eventually act — and where the endpoint, network and identity telemetry are all live
  and retained for far longer than an analysis window.
- **Thresholds are a choice.** Slow activity beats a specific counter, not detection. Long-window
  aggregation, per-source cumulative counting, rarity analysis and simple "this account has never
  done this before" logic are unaffected by pacing. Low-and-slow trades speed for a longer
  exposure window, which favours the defender who is retaining data.

## What a defender should collect

- **Process-creation and API telemetry for environment enumeration** — system-information
  queries, VM-artefact checks, debugger checks, especially clustered together.
- **Long-window baselines** alongside short-window thresholds: per-account, per-host,
  per-destination counts over days, not minutes.
- **Rarity/first-seen analytics** — "first time this account authenticated to this host", "first
  time this process made an outbound connection" — which have no threshold to slip under.
- **Retention.** The single most effective counter to pacing is keeping the data long enough to
  aggregate over the attacker's timescale rather than the tool's default window.

## What removes the gap

Pair every rate-based rule with a cumulative, long-window counterpart, and add first-seen
detections that do not depend on volume at all. Where analysis sandboxes are part of the
pipeline, treat "sample performed extensive environment checks and then exited" as a suspicious
verdict rather than a clean one.

title: Traffic obfuscation and covert channels — how it works and how it is detected
summary: Encryption, protocol mimicry, domain fronting and third-party services hide command-and-control CONTENT. They do not hide that a conversation happened — and metadata, not payload, is where network detection has lived for years.

steps.text: Collect flow metadata with duration and byte counts (Zeek conn.log or NetFlow) — beaconing analysis needs nothing more than this.
Baseline JA3/JA4 client fingerprints; a fingerprint that is not one of your standard stacks is worth investigating regardless of the SNI.
Monitor DNS query volume, label entropy and record-type mix per zone for tunnelling.
Attribute every outbound connection to a process (Sysmon 3 / auditd) — a non-browser process holding a long-lived TLS session is the anomaly.
Enforce proxy-only egress so anything reaching the internet directly is a policy violation by definition.

> **How to read this page.** This is a DEFENDER'S reference. It explains what this family of technique is and why it works — enough to recognise it — and then spends most of its length on how it is *detected* and what removes it. It is deliberately not a recipe: there are no commands here, and it will not tell you how to evade anything. If you are testing, the value is knowing what you would be leaving behind; if you are defending, the value is the telemetry and the controls.

## What it is

Making command-and-control traffic look like something else: TLS with a plausible SNI, HTTP that
mimics ordinary browsing, DNS tunnelling, traffic relayed through a proxy chain, or C2 carried
over a legitimate third-party service (a cloud drive, a paste site, a chat API). ATT&CK:
[T1573 Encrypted Channel](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1573), [T1071.001 Web Protocols](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001),
[T1090 Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090), [T1102 Web Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102) — all **Command and Control**
(TA0011).

## Why it works

It targets payload inspection. If the bytes are encrypted or the destination is a service you
cannot block, content-based signatures have nothing to match.

## Why it usually fails

Network detection largely gave up on payloads years ago. What is left is metadata, and metadata
survives every one of these techniques:

- **Beaconing rhythm.** Automated callbacks have periodicity. Even with jitter, the
  inter-arrival distribution of a beacon does not look like human browsing. This is the
  workhorse detection for the whole family.
- **Session shape.** Ratio of bytes sent to received, session duration, request sizes clustering
  around a constant — all visible in NetFlow and Zeek `conn.log` without decrypting anything.
- **TLS fingerprints.** JA3/JA4 and certificate characteristics identify the *client stack*
  regardless of what the SNI claims, which is what makes fronting and mimicry detectable.
- **DNS behaviour.** Tunnelling shows as high query volume to one zone, long or high-entropy
  labels, unusual record types and low NXDOMAIN correlation — none of which requires reading the
  payload.
- **Destination novelty.** First-seen domains, newly registered domains, and "no other host in
  the estate has ever talked to this" are strong, cheap signals.
- **Attribution to a process.** On the endpoint, Sysmon EID 3 ties the connection to the process
  that made it. A non-browser process holding a long-lived outbound TLS session is anomalous no
  matter how ordinary the traffic looks.

## What a defender should collect

- **Zeek `conn.log` / `ssl.log` / `dns.log` / `http.log`**, or equivalent NetFlow with duration
  and byte counts.
- **JA3/JA4 client fingerprints** and certificate metadata.
- **Sysmon EID 3 / auditd connect** to attribute every outbound session to a process.
- **Proxy logs** with the full URL, user-agent and destination category.
- **Egress policy** — the strongest control here is architectural: if only the proxy may reach
  the internet, everything else is a policy violation by definition.

## What removes the gap

Force egress through an inspecting proxy and alert on anything that bypasses it. Add beaconing
analysis over flow metadata, JA3/JA4 baselines, and DNS volume/entropy monitoring. None of these
require breaking encryption, which is why they keep working.

title: Persistence — how it works and how it is detected
summary: Surviving a reboot means writing something down. Every persistence mechanism is a durable change to a small, enumerable set of places — which makes this the most detectable family on the list, and the one most worth auditing after any test.

steps.text: Alert by default on service installation (7045/4697) and scheduled-task creation (4698/4702) — both are rare enough on most estates to justify it.
Snapshot every autostart location per host and DIFF it periodically; this catches mechanisms you have no specific rule for.
Put file-integrity monitoring on web roots — a new or modified script there is the web-shell detection.
Treat WMI event subscription creation (Sysmon 19/20/21) as high severity; it is rare.
Watch account-level persistence too: 4720/4728/4732/4738, plus added credentials and key-credential links in the directory.
After any authorized test, reconcile the engagement's Detection footprint against the artefacts found — every persistence artefact created must be accounted for and removed.
